Starting care

What Happens in Couples Therapy?

Prepare for the first conversation about couples therapy: each partner's goals, the therapist's process, privacy questions and whether joint work is appropriate.

About 2 minutes of article reading. Educational information, not a personal assessment.

Review draft. This article has not received clinical and publication approval.

On this page

  2. You do not need identical goals to ask questions
  3. Clarify privacy and contact before sharing sensitive information

Take these questions with you

  • How do you assess whether joint sessions are appropriate?
  • What if we have different goals?
  • What privacy and individual-contact policies will apply?

No answers are collected on this page.

Start by understanding the therapist's process

M.F.T.'s published couples work describes attention to recurring interactions, communication and emotional connection. That description is not a promise that every clinician uses the same intake format or that the relationship will have a particular outcome.

Ask the clinician how they begin, what each person will be invited to discuss, and how they decide whether working together is appropriate. You can ask about the process before agreeing to it.

Background sources [1]

You do not need identical goals to ask questions

As an optional preparation step, privately identify what made you consider therapy and what you are uncertain about. One person may want help discussing conflict; another may want clarity about whether to continue the relationship. These are illustrative possibilities, not assumptions about you. Ask how a clinician would handle different goals rather than pretending they are already aligned.

You might bring one ordinary interaction you would like help understanding, but you do not need to assemble evidence to win an argument. Ask how each person's experience will be heard and how the therapist manages interruptions or overwhelming discussions.

Clarify privacy and contact before sharing sensitive information

Ask about the clinician's policies for individual conversations within couples work, information shared outside joint sessions, records, and messages between appointments. Do not assume a universal secrets policy. Request a clear explanation of the actual agreement before relying on it.

Also ask how to raise a safety concern privately and whether separate support or another service might be more appropriate. A first inquiry does not obligate you to attend jointly, disclose something unsafe in front of a partner, or commit to staying together.

At M.F.T.: couples appointments are private pay

Couples consultations and couples sessions are private pay. Confirm the appointment type, fee and clinician availability before requesting a time. This relationship guide is educational; it is not an assessment result or a substitute for individualized care.

Safety comes before joint work

Fear, threats or control call for private support, not a shared communication exercise. The Hotline offers confidential support. [2]
